gancho: No kabuki, teatro japonês, homens fazem os papéis femininos. Mas quem o criou foi uma mulher, Izumo no Okuni, com uma trupe só de atrizes. Em 1629, o xogunato proibiu as mulheres de atuar nele.
explicacao: Pouco se sabe com certeza sobre a vida dela, mas, segundo os relatos, Okuni nasceu por volta de 1578 perto do grande santuário de Izumo, onde serviu como miko, uma sacerdotisa auxiliar, conhecida pelo talento para dançar e representar. Mandada a Kyoto para dançar e arrecadar doações para o santuário, por volta de 1603 começou a se apresentar no leito seco do rio Kamo. Reuniu mulheres marginalizadas, muitas ligadas à prostituição, e ensinou a elas canto, dança e atuação. Como a trupe era só feminina, as atrizes também faziam os homens. O público chamou aquilo de kabuki, palavra ligada à excentricidade e à ousadia das apresentações. O sucesso foi copiado por bordéis, e as brigas entre homens disputando as atrizes somaram-se aos pedidos de reforma moral: em 1629, o xógum Tokugawa Iemitsu proibiu as mulheres no kabuki. Rapazes as substituíram e logo foram proibidos pelos mesmos motivos, e o palco ficou restrito a homens adultos, regra que os teatros oficiais seguem até hoje. Os atores especializados em papéis femininos se chamam onnagata, "papel de mulher", e treinam por anos maquiagem, postura e uma voz em falsete. A proibição às mulheres caiu na era Meiji, mas atrizes no kabuki continuaram raras.

fontes.trecho: Izumo no Okuni (出雲 阿国) was a Japanese entertainer and miko (shrine maiden) who is believed to have invented the theatrical art form of kabuki. [...] Born c. 1578, Okuni grew up in the vicinity of the Izumo shrine [...] Eventually, Okuni joined as a miko (shrine maiden), where she was known for her skill in dancing and acting, as well as her beauty. As it was customary to send priests and others to solicit contributions for the shrine, she was sent to Kyoto to perform sacred dances and songs. [...] Around 1603, Okuni began performing on the dry riverbed of the Shijōgawara (Fourth Street Dry Riverbed) of the Kamo River and at Kitano Shrine. [...] Gathering up the female outcasts and misfits of the region, particularly those involved in prostitution, Okuni gave them direction, teaching them acting, dancing and singing skills in order to form her troupe. [...] others labelled Okuni's troupe performances "kabuki" due to their eccentricity and social daring. [...] Okuni's troupe was exclusively female. Thus, she required her actresses to play both male and female roles. As her troupe gained fame, she was emulated by many others, particularly brothels [...] In 1629, due to outcry for moral reform and concern about fights breaking out between men trying to win the attention of the actresses, shōgun Tokugawa Iemitsu forbade women from performing in kabuki. They were quickly replaced by young men as actors and "actresses", though this was soon banned as well due to some of the same issues of sex work and 'corruption of morals', restricting the performances to those by older men, which is a standing practice in the official theatres even today. [...] Few concrete details are known about her life

Onnagata (女形/女方, lit. 'female role'), also oyama (女形, lit. 'female form'), are male actors who play female roles in kabuki theatre. The practice originated in 1629 after women were banned from performing in kabuki performances. [...] During the Meiji era, the ban on women performing was lifted, and women began performing in kabuki performances where they played onnagata roles. This was more uncommon [...] Some of the techniques that onnagata actors have to master with years of training and research include being able to move gracefully across the stage when wearing geta, adopting a more feminine posture [...] and speaking at a higher pitch (falsetto) throughout the entire performance.

gancho: A estreia de "A Sagração da Primavera", em 1913, é contada como um motim. Mas a palavra só surgiu mais de uma década depois, a polícia na sala nunca foi confirmada e o balé foi até o fim, com aplausos.
explicacao: O balé de Stravinsky, com coreografia de Nijinsky, estreou em 29 de maio de 1913 no Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, em Paris. Houve barulho de verdade: risos já na introdução, gritaria que impedia os bailarinos de ouvir a música e, segundo o regente Pierre Monteux, objetos atirados contra a orquestra. Stravinsky saiu da plateia e viu o resto da coxia, onde Nijinsky gritava a contagem dos passos. Cerca de quarenta dos mais exaltados foram retirados, talvez com ajuda da polícia, o que nenhum registro confirma. Mas a apresentação não parou, a segunda parte foi bem mais calma e, no fim, dançarinos, orquestra, Stravinsky e Nijinsky voltaram várias vezes ao palco para agradecer. Vários detalhes famosos não resistem às fontes. O escritor Carl Van Vechten contou que um vizinho de poltrona batucou em sua cabeça, mas numa carta de 1916, só publicada em 2013, admitiu que tinha ido à segunda noite. A saída furiosa do compositor Saint-Saëns também é lenda: ele nem estava lá. E, segundo o musicólogo Richard Taruskin, o que chocou foi menos a música que a coreografia, com seus passos pesados e batidos no chão.

fontes.trecho: the original choreography was by Vaslav Nijinsky with stage designs and costumes by Nicholas Roerich. When first performed at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées on 29 May 1913, the avant-garde nature of the music and choreography caused a sensation. Many have called the first-night reaction a "riot" or "near-riot", though this wording did not come about until reviews of later performances in 1924, over a decade later. [...] Some eyewitnesses and commentators said that the disturbances in the audience began during the Introduction, and grew noisier when the curtain rose on the stamping dancers in "Augurs of Spring". But Taruskin asserts, "it was not Stravinsky's music that did the shocking. It was the ugly earthbound lurching and stomping devised by Vaslav Nijinsky." Marie Rambert, who was working as an assistant to Nijinsky, recalled later that it was soon impossible to hear the music on the stage. In his autobiography, Stravinsky writes that the derisive laughter that greeted the first bars of the Introduction disgusted him, and that he left the auditorium to watch the rest of the performance from the stage wings. The demonstrations, he says, grew into "a terrific uproar" which, along with the on-stage noises, drowned out the voice of Nijinsky who was shouting the step numbers to the dancers. Two years after the premiere the journalist and photographer Carl Van Vechten claimed in his book Music After the Great War that the person behind him became carried away with excitement, and "began to beat rhythmically on top of my head with his fists". In 1916, in a letter not published until 2013, Van Vechten admitted he had actually attended the second night, among other changes of fact. [...] "Everything available was tossed in our direction, but we continued to play on". Around forty of the worst offenders were ejected [...] possibly with the intervention of the police, although this is uncorroborated. Through all the disturbances the performance continued without interruption. The unrest receded significantly during Part II [...] At the end there were several curtain calls for the dancers, for Monteux and the orchestra, and for Stravinsky and Nijinsky [...] Of later reports that the veteran composer Camille Saint-Saëns had stormed out of the premiere, Stravinsky observed that this was impossible; Saint-Saëns did not attend.

gancho: As primeiras bailarinas a ficar na ponta dos pés eram erguidas por uma "máquina voadora" de fios. Depois vieram sapatilhas de cetim cerzido, sem apoio. A biqueira rígida só surgiu no fim do século XIX.
explicacao: Em 1681, quando as bailarinas passaram a se apresentar nos palcos de balé, os sapatos de dança femininos tinham salto. Nos anos 1730, Marie Camargo, da Ópera de Paris, foi a primeira a dançar sem salto, o que permitia saltos difíceis de fazer antes, e depois da Revolução Francesa o salto sumiu de vez. Em 1796, Charles Didelot criou uma "máquina voadora" que suspendia as bailarinas, que assim ficavam na ponta dos pés antes de deixar o chão. O público adorou a leveza, e os coreógrafos passaram a querer mais trabalho de ponta, agora sem fios. Quando Marie Taglioni dançou "La Sylphide" na ponta, suas sapatilhas eram chinelos de cetim adaptados, com sola de couro e as laterais e a ponta cerzidas para manter a forma. Sem nenhum apoio, as bailarinas acolchoavam os dedos e dependiam só da força dos pés e tornozelos. No fim do século XIX, na Itália, bailarinas como Pierina Legnani passaram a usar sapatilhas com uma plataforma plana na frente, uma caixa de camadas de tecido envolvendo os dedos e sola mais firme. A sapatilha moderna costuma ser atribuída a Anna Pavlova, que tinha o peito do pé muito arqueado e, para se proteger, pôs solas de couro endurecido e achatou a ponta.

fontes.trecho: Women began to dance ballet in 1681, twenty years after King Louis XIV of France ordered the founding of the Académie Royale de Danse. At that time, the standard women's ballet shoe had heels. In the 1730s, dancer Marie Camargo of the Paris Opéra Ballet was the first to wear a non-heeled shoe, enabling her to perform leaps that would have been difficult, if not impossible, in the more conventional shoes of the age. After the French Revolution, heels were completely eliminated from standard ballet shoes. [...] The first dancers to rise up on their toes did so with the help of an invention by Charles Didelot in 1796. His "flying machine" lifted dancers upward, allowing them to stand on their toes before leaving the ground. This lightness and ethereal quality was well received by audiences and, as a result, choreographers began to look for ways to incorporate more pointe work into their pieces. As dance progressed into the 19th century, the emphasis on technical skill increased, as did the desire to dance en pointe without the aid of wires. When Marie Taglioni first danced La Sylphide en pointe, her shoes were nothing more than modified satin slippers; the soles were made of leather and the sides and toes were darned to help the shoes hold their shapes. Because the shoes of this period offered no support, dancers would pad their toes for comfort and rely on the strength of their feet and ankles for support. The next substantially different form of pointe shoe appeared in Italy in the late 19th century. Dancers like Pierina Legnani wore shoes with a sturdy, flat platform at the front end of the shoe, rather than the more sharply pointed toe of earlier models. These shoes also included a box [...] made of layers of fabric [...] for containing the toes, and a stiffer, stronger sole. [...] The birth of the modern pointe shoe is often attributed to the early 20th-century Russian ballerina Anna Pavlova [...] Pavlova had particularly high, arched insteps, which left her vulnerable to injury when dancing en pointe. [...] To compensate for this, she inserted toughened leather soles into her shoes for extra support and flattened and hardened the toe area to form a box.

gancho: Em 1613, um canhão de cena incendiou o teatro Globe, de Shakespeare. Segundo um relato, só um homem se feriu, e as calças dele foram apagadas com cerveja. A réplica de 1997 voltou a ter telhado de palha.
explicacao: Em 29 de junho de 1613, durante uma apresentação de "Henrique VIII", um canhão usado como efeito falhou e pôs fogo nas vigas de madeira e no telhado de palha. Um dos poucos documentos que sobraram diz que ninguém se machucou, exceto um homem cujas calças em chamas foram apagadas com uma garrafa de cerveja. O teatro foi refeito no ano seguinte, agora com telhado de telhas, fechado na guerra civil inglesa e demolido por volta de 1644–45. Em 1970, o ator americano Sam Wanamaker criou uma fundação para erguer uma réplica fiel perto do local original. Muitos diziam que era impossível conciliar o projeto do século XVI com as normas contra incêndio, mas ele insistiu por mais de 20 anos. Wanamaker morreu em 1993, e a nova casa abriu em 1997, a cerca de 230 metros do terreno antigo. É toda de carvalho inglês, com encaixes de madeira e sem aço estrutural. E tem o que se diz ser o primeiro e único telhado de palha permitido em Londres desde o Grande Incêndio de 1666. A palha recebe produtos antichama, e há sprinklers no telhado. Pela segurança, cabem 1.400 espectadores, contra 3.000 no teatro original.

fontes.trecho: On 29 June 1613, the Globe Theatre went up in flames during a performance of Henry VIII. A theatrical cannon, set off during the performance, misfired, igniting the wooden beams and thatching. According to one of the few surviving documents of the event, no one was hurt except a man whose burning breeches were put out with a bottle of ale. It was rebuilt in the following year (with a tile roof) at a cost of £1,400. Like all the other theatres in London, the Globe was closed down by the outbreak of the First English Civil War [...] It was pulled down in 1644–45 (the commonly cited document dating the act to 15 April 1644 is not reliable)

The original globe theatre was built in 1599 by the Lord Chamberlain's Men, destroyed by a fire in 1613, rebuilt in 1614, and then demolished in 1644. [...] It is considered quite realistic, though modern safety requirements mean that it accommodates only 1,400 spectators compared to the original theatre's 3,000. The modern Shakespeare's Globe was founded by the actor and director Sam Wanamaker, and built about 230 metres (750 ft) from the site of the original theatre in the historic open-air style. It opened to the public in 1997 [...] In 1970, American actor and director Sam Wanamaker, who had emigrated to London in the 1950s, founded the Shakespeare Globe Trust and the International Shakespeare Globe Centre, with the objective of building a faithful recreation of Shakespeare's Globe close to its original location at Bankside, Southwark. [...] Many people maintained that a faithful Globe reconstruction was impossible to achieve due to the complications in the 16th-century design and modern fire safety requirements; however, Wanamaker and his associate Diana Devlin persevered in their vision for over 20 years to create the theatre. [...] rely of English oak, with mortise and tenon joints and is, in this sense, an "authentic" 16th-century timber-framed building as no structural steel was used. [...] the Globe has what has been claimed to be the first and only thatched roof permitted in London since the Great Fire of London in 1666. The modern thatch is well protected by fire retardants, and sprinklers on the roof ensure further protection against fire.
Wanamaker died of lung cancer in London on December 18, 1993, aged 74, before the grand opening of the Globe by Queen Elizabeth II on June 12, 1997.

gancho: Na primeira edição impressa de "Hamlet", de 1603, o monólogo famoso diz: "Ser ou não ser, sim, eis o ponto. Morrer, dormir, é só isso? Sim, só isso". Esse texto só veio à tona em 1823, e sua origem ainda é discutida.
explicacao: "Hamlet" sobreviveu em três versões antigas, todas diferentes: o Primeiro Quarto, de 1603; o Segundo Quarto, de 1604; e o Primeiro Fólio, de 1623. Cada uma tem trechos que faltam nas outras. O Primeiro Quarto, apelidado de "quarto ruim", tem pouco mais da metade do texto do segundo e ficou perdido até 1823; só restam dois exemplares. Nele, o monólogo mais famoso do teatro segue por outro caminho: "Morrer, dormir, é só isso? Sim, só isso". De onde veio esse texto é uma questão em aberto. Uma hipótese é que seja uma reconstrução de memória feita por um ator de papel pequeno, provavelmente o que fazia Marcelo, e os estudiosos discordam se foi pirataria ou algo autorizado. Outras propostas: um rascunho inicial de Shakespeare, uma adaptação ou uma versão encurtada para companhias em turnê. A capa do Segundo Quarto anuncia um texto "aumentado em quase o mesmo tanto", provavelmente uma comparação com o primeiro. Apesar da fama ruim, o Primeiro Quarto traz rubricas que mostram como a peça era encenada, uma cena que não existe nas outras versões e um enredo mais linear, e já teve pelo menos 28 montagens desde 1881.

fontes.trecho: Three different early versions of the play are extant: the First Quarto (Q1, 1603); the Second Quarto (Q2, 1604); and the First Folio (F1, 1623). Each version includes lines and passages missing from the others. [...] the so-called "bad" first quarto, under the name The Tragicall Historie of Hamlet Prince of Denmarke. Q1 contains just over half of the text of the later second quarto. [...] Q1 was discovered in 1823. Only two copies are extant. [...] Yet Q1 has value: it contains stage directions (such as Ophelia entering with a lute and her hair down) that reveal actual stage practices in a way that Q2 and F1 do not; it contains an entire scene (usually labelled 4.6) that does not appear in either Q2 or F1 [...] the opening lines of the famous "To be, or not to be" soliloquy: "To be, or not to be, aye there's the point. / To die, to sleep, is that all? Aye all: [...] That Q1 is so much shorter than Q2 has spurred speculation that Q1 is an early draft, or perhaps an adaptation, a bootleg copy, or a stage adaptation. On the title page of Q2, its text is described as "newly imprinted and enlarged to almost as much again as it was". That is probably a comparison t [...] Q1's more linear plot design is certainly easier [...] may be a memorial reconstruction of the play as Shakespeare's company performed it, by an actor who played a minor role (most likely Marcellus). Scholars disagree whether the reconstruction was pirated or authorised. It is suggested by Irace that Q1 is an abridged version intended especially for travelling productions [...] has led to at least 28 different Q1 productions since 1881.

gancho: No nô japonês, os atores aprendem que erguer certas máscaras as deixa alegres e baixá-las as deixa tristes. Em laboratório, porém, voluntários viram o contrário, e a explicação parece estar na penumbra do palco.
explicacao: O nô é uma forma de teatro dançado encenada desde o século XIV, e em geral só o ator principal, o shite, usa máscara. Esculpidas em cipreste japonês, as máscaras estilizam a expressão em vez de eliminá-la, e algumas usam a luz para mudar de emoção. Pela convenção do palco, erguer levemente o rosto, gesto chamado de "iluminar" a máscara, revela traços que parecem sorrir; baixá-lo, "nublando" a máscara, a deixa triste ou zangada. Quando cientistas testaram isso, o resultado saiu invertido. Em 2000, Lyons e colegas viram que participantes britânicos e japoneses achavam alegre a máscara inclinada para baixo e triste a inclinada para cima, e outros estudos acharam a mesma tendência. Em 2013, Kawai e colegas mostraram que basta sobrepor à foto frontal de uma máscara as sombras dela inclinada para obter o mesmo efeito. A pista está na boca: inclinada para baixo, a máscara fica com os cantos dos lábios puxados para cima, como num sorriso, e um estudo de Miyata e colegas apontou a boca como o traço decisivo para julgar a emoção de uma máscara. No teatro, porém, o palco é escuro e cheio de sombras, e o público vê os atores de longe. Os autores sugerem que, ali, o formato da boca nem sempre fica visível, e a máscara inclinada para baixo pode não parecer alegre. Vista de perto, numa tela, a boca passa a dominar.

fontes.trecho: is a major form of classical Japanese dance-drama that has been performed since the 14th century. It is Japan's oldest major theater art that is still regularly performed today. [...] Noh masks (能面 nō-men or 面 omote) are carved from blocks of Japanese cypress (檜 "hinoki"), and painted with natural pigments on a neutral base of glue and crushed seashell. There are approximately 450 different masks mostly based on sixty types, all of which have distinctive names. [...] Noh masks signify the characters' gender, age, and social ranking, and by wearing masks the actors may portray youngsters, old men, female, or nonhuman (divine or demonic) characters. Only the shite, the main actor, wears a mask in most plays [...] the use of the mask in Noh is not an abandonment of facial expressions altogether. Rather, its intent is to stylize and codify the facial expressions through the use of the mask and to stimulate the imagination of the audience. [...] Some masks use lighting effect to convey different emotions through slight tilting of the head. Facing slightly upward, or "brightening" the mask, will let the mask to capture more light, revealing more features that appear laughing or smiling. Facing downward, or "clouding" it, will cause the mask to appear sad or mad. Noh masks are treasured by Noh families and institutions, and the powerful Noh schools hold the oldest and most valuable Noh masks in their private collections, rarely seen by the public.

fontes.titulo: Shadows Alter Facial Expressions of Noh Masks (Kawai et al., PLoS ONE, 2013)
fontes.trecho: Experiment 2 further revealed that frontal Noh mask images having shadows of upward/downward tilted masks were evaluated as sad/happy, respectively. This was consistent with outcomes from preceding studies using actually tilted Noh mask images. [...] Using Noh masks as facial stimuli, Lyons et al. [5] showed that both British and Japanese participants attributed happiness to a downward tilted mask, and sadness to an upward tilted mask. [...] Miyata et al. [9] further demonstrated that different facial parts convey different emotions in a Noh mask, and that among the facial parts the mouth serves as a diagnostic feature in the categorical judgment of emotions. [...] The studies, however, revealed trends opposite to the convention of the Noh drama. That is, the mask is tilted upwards/downwards when signifying a happy/sad state, the gestures known as terasu (shining) and kumorasu (clouding), respectively [...] Specifically, the corners of the lips are pulled up for the downward tilted Noh mask, which are elements of a happy expression [...] In addition, the Noh stage is dark and full of shadows, and observers see the actors from a relatively distant location. Thus, during the actual Noh play, the shape of the mouth is not necessarily apparent from the observer [...] viewpoint, where downward tilted masks may not be likely to look happy. However, when closely looking at the mask alone on a computer monitor, as done in the present study, the shape of the mouth should clearly serve as a distinctive feature in the recognition of emotions [...] Lyons MJ, Campbell R, Plante A, Coleman M, Kamachi M, et al. (2000) The Noh mask effect [...] Kawai N, Miyata H, Nishimura R, Okanoya K (2013) Shadows Alter Facial Expressions of Noh Masks.

gancho: Zeami, o grande mestre do nô, escreveu no século XV tratados sobre a arte do ator pensados só para a sua trupe. Por séculos quase ninguém os leu, até que alguns apareceram num sebo japonês em 1908.
explicacao: Zeami nasceu em 1363, perto de Nara, e atuava na trupe do pai, Kan'ami. Os dois deram forma ao nô, com o apoio do xógum Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, que se encantou pelo jovem ator. Ao longo de cerca de quatro décadas, Zeami escreveu 21 textos críticos sobre a formação do ator, a interpretação de personagens, a música e o movimento, e também sobre como viver. Não eram para o público: as trupes eram hereditárias, e esse saber passava de geração em geração dentro delas. O primeiro tratado, o Fūshikaden, é o mais antigo tratado de teatro conhecido no Japão. A sorte de Zeami virou com outro xógum, Yoshinori, que em 1434 o mandou para o exílio na ilha de Sado. Depois da morte de Zeami, em 1443, os tratados ficaram ao alcance só da elite guerreira. Em 1908, vários deles foram encontrados numa loja de livros usados no Japão, e só então começaram a circular. A coleção completa saiu apenas em 1940. As peças, ao contrário, nunca deixaram de ser encenadas.

fontes.trecho: Yoshinori sent Zeami into exile to Sado Island. After Yoshinori's death in 1441, Zeami returned to mainland Japan, where he died in 1443. [...] The Shōgun was impressed by the young actor and began a close relationship with him. [...] Zeami was born in 1363 near Nara [...] Zeami produced 21 critical writings over a period of roughly four decades. His treatises discuss the principles of Noh. He sought to inform his colleagues of the most important aspects of theater, discussing the education of the actor, character acting, music, and physical movement. His writings also discussed broader themes, such as how life should be lived. The treatises were intended for a small circle of his colleagues, since the troupes were hereditary, and such information was traditionally passed down between generations. [...] It is the first known treatise on drama in Japan [...] In 1434, Zeami was exiled to Sado Island. [...] Zeami's treatises were not widely available after his death; only the upper-class warriors were able to gain access to them. In 1908, several of the treatises were discovered at a used books store in Japan. They gained wider circulation after this discovery, but a complete set was not published until 1940. However, Zeami's plays have been continually performed in Japan since they were first written.

In 14th century, with strong support and patronage from shōgun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, Zeami was able to establish Noh as the most prominent theatre art form of the time. [...] Kan'ami Kiyotsugu and his son Zeami Motokiyo reinterpreted various traditional performing arts and completed Noh in a

gancho: "Slapstick", nome em inglês do humor de tapas e trombadas, era um objeto: um bastão de duas ripas da commedia dell'arte que estala alto ao acertar um ator, quase sem machucar.
explicacao: Na Itália do século XVI, as trupes da commedia dell'arte usavam o batacchio, um porrete feito de duas ripas finas de madeira presas juntas. Ao acertar alguém, ele produz um estalo forte, mas quase nenhuma força chega ao corpo do outro ator. Assim, os atores podiam se bater várias vezes em cena, com grande efeito sonoro e quase nenhuma dor. Em inglês, o objeto virou "slap stick", algo como "bastão de tapa", e o nome passou a designar todo o gênero de comédia física exagerada. Junto com a bexiga inflável, antepassada da almofada de pum, o bastão está entre os primeiros efeitos especiais. Ele também sobreviveu no teatro de bonecos de Punch e Judy, registrado na Inglaterra pela primeira vez em 9 de maio de 1662, em que Punch distribui pancadas com um grande bastão. O gênero passou depois pelo teatro de variedades inglês, onde Charlie Chaplin e Stan Laurel aprenderam o ofício; os quinze anos de Chaplin no music hall marcaram a comédia de todos os seus filmes.

fontes.trecho: Slapstick is a style of humor involving exaggerated physical activity that exceeds the boundaries of normal physical comedy [...] The term arises from a device developed for use in the broad, physical comedy style known as commedia dell'arte in 16th-century Italy. The "slap stick" consists of two thin slats of wood, which makes a "slap" when striking another actor, with little force needed to make a loud—and comical—sound. [...] The name "slapstick" originates from the Italian batacchio or bataccio [...] called the "slap stick" in English [...] a club-like object composed of two wooden slats used in commedia dell'arte. When struck, the Batacchio produces a loud smacking noise, though it is only a little force that is transferred from the object to the person being struck. Actors may thus hit one another repeatedly with great audible effect while causing no damage and only very minor, if any, pain. Along with the inflatable bladder (of which the whoopee cushion is a modern variant), it was among the earliest special effects. [...] In Punch and Judy shows, which first appeared in England on 9 May 1662, a large slapstick is wielded by Punch against the other characters. [...] British comedians who honed their skills at pantomime and music hall sketches include Charlie Chaplin, Stan Laurel [...] Chaplin's fifteen-year music hall career inspired the comedy in all his later film work

gancho: "A Ratoeira", de Agatha Christie, estreou em Londres em 1952 e passou de 30 mil sessões: é a peça há mais tempo em cartaz no mundo. A autora apostava em oito meses. Os direitos foram presente a um neto de nove anos.
explicacao: A história nasceu como uma radionovela curta, "Three Blind Mice", escrita como presente de aniversário para a rainha Mary e transmitida em 1947. A versão para o palco teve de mudar de nome, e "The Mousetrap" foi sugestão do genro da autora. A temporada londrina começou em 25 de novembro de 1952 no Ambassadors Theatre e, em 1974, passou para o teatro vizinho, o St Martin's, sem interromper a série. Na autobiografia, Christie conta que o produtor previu catorze meses em cartaz e ela respondeu que não duraria tanto, talvez oito. Quando escreveu a peça, deu os direitos ao neto Mathew Prichard como presente de aniversário; ele tinha nove anos e, adulto, criou uma fundação que usa o dinheiro para apoiar as artes, sobretudo no País de Gales. A longevidade travou até o cinema: os direitos de filmagem foram comprados em 1956, mas o contrato só permite um filme depois que a montagem de Londres sair de cartaz por pelo menos seis meses, e a peça nunca encerrou a temporada. Nem a pandemia encerrou oficialmente a temporada: as sessões ficaram suspensas por 14 meses, de março de 2020 a maio de 2021, e a mesma montagem voltou ao palco do St Martin's. Por tradição, o público é convidado a não revelar o final.

fontes.trecho: The play opened in London's West End in 1952, and is the longest-running West End show, with over 30,000 performances, making it the longest run of any play in the world. While pandemic closures suspended performances between March 2020 and May 2021 [...] the play has a twist ending which the audience are traditionally asked not to reveal after leaving the theatre. [...] The play began life as a short radio play written by Agatha Christie as a birthday present for Queen Mary, the consort of King George V. It was broadcast on 30 May 1947 under the name Three Blind Mice. [...] When she wrote the play, Christie gave the rights to her grandson Mathew Prichard as a birthday present. [...] no film adaptation can be produced until the West End production has been closed for at least six months. Producer John Woolf bought the film rights to the play in 1956, but Woolf and his heirs have been unable to produce an adaptation because the play has never closed. [...] The play had to be renamed at the insistence of Emile Littler [...] The suggestion to call it The Mousetrap came from Christie's son-in-law, Anthony Hicks. [...] before it began its run in London on 25 November 1952 at the Ambassadors Theatre. It ran at this theatre until Saturday, 23 March 1974 when it immediately transferred to the larger St Martin's Theatre, next door, where it reopened on Monday, 25 March, thus keeping its "initial run" status. [...] In her autobiography, she reports a conversation that she had with Peter Saunders: "Fourteen months I am going to give it", says Saunders. To which Christie replies, "It won't run that long. Eight months perhaps. Yes, I think eight months." [...] Prichard, who was only nine when he was given the copyright of the play, set up the Colwinston Charitable Trust in 1995 to use the money from productions of the play. The trust supports charities for the arts, mainly in Wales. [...] Performances at the St. Martin's Theatre were halted on 16 March 2020, along with all other West End shows, during the COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom. The Mousetrap re-opened on 17 May 2021 after 14 months without performances.

gancho: A expressão inglesa "in the limelight", estar em evidência, vem de uma luz de palco do século XIX: uma chama de oxigênio e hidrogênio esquentava um bloco de cal virgem até ele brilhar intensamente.
explicacao: Em inglês, "lime" é cal, e a limelight era exatamente isso: uma chama alimentada por oxigênio e hidrogênio apontada para um cilindro de cal virgem, o óxido de cálcio, que passava a emitir uma luz branca e forte. O efeito foi descoberto nos anos 1820 por Goldsworthy Gurney. Em 1825, o engenheiro escocês Thomas Drummond viu uma demonstração feita por Michael Faraday e pensou primeiro num uso bem longe do teatro: a topografia. Construiu um aparelho que funcionava em 1826, e por isso a luz também ficou conhecida como luz de Drummond. O primeiro uso conhecido num espetáculo foi ao ar livre, em 1836, num píer do condado de Kent, para iluminar um malabarista. No ano seguinte, chegou ao palco do teatro de Covent Garden, em Londres, e nas décadas de 1860 e 1870 se espalhou pelos teatros do mundo, servindo para destacar um artista sozinho em cena, como os refletores de hoje. Também iluminou alvos na Guerra Civil Americana. A luz elétrica a aposentou, mas a expressão ficou, e o apelido "limes" passou para os refletores elétricos.

fontes.trecho: Limelight  (also known as Drummond light or calcium light) is a non-electric type of stage lighting that was once used in theatres and music halls. An intense illumination is created when a flame fed by oxygen and hydrogen is directed at a cylinder of quicklime (calcium oxide), due to a combination of incandescence and candoluminescence. Although it has long since been replaced by electric lighting, the term has survived, as someone in the public eye is still said to be "in the limelight". The actual lamps are called "limes", a term which has been transferred to electrical equivalents. [...] The limelight effect was discovered in the 1820s by Goldsworthy Gurney [...] In 1825, Scottish engineer Thomas Drummond (1797–1840) saw a demonstration of the effect by Michael Faraday and realized that the light would be useful for surveying. Drummond built a working version in 1826. The device is sometimes called the Drummond light after his adaptation of Gurney's discovery. [...] The earliest known use of limelight at a public performance was outdoors, over Herne Bay Pier, Kent, on the night of 3 October 1836, to illuminate a juggling performance by magician Ching Lau Lauro. [...] Limelight was first used for indoor stage illumination in the Covent Garden Theatre in London in 1837 and enjoyed widespread use in theatres around the world in the 1860s and 1870s. Limelights were employed to highlight solo performers in the same manner as modern spotlights. [...] During the American Civil War, in July and August 1863, calcium lights were used during the siege of Fort Wagner, allowing Union forces to illuminate their artillery target at night [...] Limelight technology was gradually replaced by electric arc lighting

gancho: Aos catorze anos, Luís XIV dançou o papel do Sol nascente num balé que durava 13 horas. Dançou 80 papéis ao longo da vida e usou a dança como instrumento de poder sobre a nobreza.
explicacao: O "Ballet Royal de la Nuit" estreou em Paris em 23 de fevereiro de 1653. O espetáculo atravessava as quatro vigílias da noite, das 6 da tarde às 6 da manhã, com quarenta e cinco entradas e personagens como deusas, lobisomens, bruxas, mendigos e ladrões. No fim, com o raiar do dia, surgia o rei adolescente como Apolo, o sol nascente, imagem que realçava o poder da monarquia e sua proximidade com o divino. Não foi caso isolado: Luís XIV dançou 80 papéis em 40 grandes balés, uma carreira próxima à de um bailarino profissional, incluindo papéis em comédias-balés de Molière. A dança também era política. O rei a integrou à vida da corte e manteve os nobres ocupados com o rigor da etiqueta dos passos, longe da política. Em 1661, fundou a Academia Real de Dança e mandou seu professor, Pierre Beauchamp, criar um sistema para registrar as coreografias no papel, publicado por Feuillet em 1700. Beauchamp também fixou as cinco posições do corpo.

fontes.trecho: which premiered on February 23, 1653, at the Salle du Petit-Bourbon in Paris. It took 13 hours to perform and included the debut of the fourteen-year-old Louis XIV as Apollo, the Sun King (Le Roi Soleil). [...] The Ballet de la Nuit concerned the four Watches (veilles) of the night, beginning at 6 o'clock in the evening and ending at 6 o'clock in the morning [...] it was an extravagant court spectacle featuring forty-five entrees and three ballets within a ballet, which took about 13 hours to perform. The plot included mythological goddesses such as Venus and Diana, werewolves, demonic creatures and witches who celebrated a black Sabbath in the horrors of the night. Shepherds, gypsies, thieves, lamplighters, beggars and crippled are among the "realistic" characters of the play. King Louis XIV appears with the coming of the day as the sun god Apollo, one of his many personifications as the rising sun, emphasizing the power of the monarchy and its closeness to the divine.

Louis was an eager dancer who performed 80 roles in 40 major ballets. This approaches the career of a professional ballet dancer. [...] He danced four parts in three of Molière's comédies-ballets [...] Ballet dancing was used by Louis as a political tool to hold power over his state. He integrated ballet deeply into court social functions and fixated his nobles' attention on upholding standards in ballet dancing, effectively distracting them from political activities. In 1661, the Royal Academy of Dance was founded by Louis to further his ambition. Pierre Beauchamp, his private dance instructor, was ordered by Louis to come up with a notation system to record ballet performances, which he did with great success. His work was adopted and published by Feuillet in 1700 as Choregraphie. [...] All the details and rules were compressed in five positions of the bodies codified by Beauchamp.

gancho: De 1660 a 1843, só uns poucos teatros com licença real podiam encenar drama "sério" em Londres. Os outros acabaram driblando a lei pondo música sob as falas, e adotaram para isso um nome francês: melodrama.
explicacao: Os puritanos tinham proibido o teatro na Inglaterra. Quando a monarquia voltou, em 1660, Carlos II deu cartas-patentes a Thomas Killigrew e William Davenant, com o monopólio de duas companhias londrinas autorizadas a encenar drama "sério". Elas se instalaram no Theatre Royal, em Drury Lane, e num antigo salão de jogo de péla, de onde a segunda companhia se mudou em 1720 para o teatro de Covent Garden, hoje a Royal Opera House. Como as duas fechavam no verão, o Haymarket virou a terceira casa com patente, em 1766, e algumas outras cidades receberam uma cada. Os demais teatros podiam apresentar comédia, pantomima e peças com música. A saída foi encenar dramas acompanhados de música do começo ao fim e chamá-los por um termo emprestado do francês: melodrama. Por isso, no sentido histórico, melodramas são dramas vitorianos em que orquestra ou canções acompanhavam a ação. O monopólio só caiu com a Lei dos Teatros de 1843, que liberou o drama para todos. A censura das peças pelo Lorde Camareiro, criada em 1737, durou bem mais: até 1968.

fontes.trecho: In scholarly and historical musical contexts, melodramas are specifically Victorian dramas in which orchestral music or song was used to accompany the action. [...] After the English Restoration of Charles II in 1660 lifted the Puritan ban on theatre, most British theatres were prohibited from performing "serious" drama but were permitted to show comedy or plays with music. Charles II issued letters patent to permit only two London theatre companies to perform "serious" drama. These were the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane and Lisle's Tennis Court in Lincoln's Inn Fields, the latter of which moved to the Theatre Royal, Covent Garden in 1720 (now the Royal Opera House). The two patent theatres closed in the summer months. To fill the gap, the Theatre Royal, Haymarket became a third patent theatre in London in 1766. Further letters patent were eventually granted to one theatre in each of several other British towns and cities. Other theatres presented dramas that were underscored with music and, borrowing the French term, called it melodrama to get around the restriction. The Theatres Act 1843 finally allowed all theatres to play drama.

Other theatres were prohibited from performing such "serious" drama, but were permitted to show comedy, pantomime or melodrama. [...] Public entertainments, such as theatrical performances, were banned under the Puritan rule in the English Commonwealth. After he was restored to the throne, Charles II issued letters patent to Thomas Killigrew and William Davenant, granting them the monopoly right to form two London theatre companies to perform "serious" drama. [...] These monopolies on the performance of "serious" plays were eventually revoked by the Theatres Act 1843, but censorship of the content of plays by the Lord Chamberlain under Robert Walpole's Theatrical Licensing Act 1737 continued until 1968.

gancho: A barra que abre portas de saída com um empurrão nasceu de tragédias em casas de espetáculo. Numa delas, em 1883, 183 crianças morreram esmagadas contra uma porta trancada após um show infantil.
explicacao: Em 16 de junho de 1883, o Victoria Hall, em Sunderland, na Inglaterra, recebeu um espetáculo de variedades para crianças. No fim, anunciou-se que alguns ingressos numerados dariam prêmios na saída, enquanto os artistas distribuíam presentes do palco. Com medo de ficar sem nada, boa parte das cerca de 1.100 crianças da galeria correu escada abaixo. Lá embaixo, a porta abria para dentro e estava trancada com ferrolho, deixando passar uma criança por vez, provavelmente para conferir os ingressos. As da frente foram esmagadas pela massa que vinha atrás, e os adultos do outro lado não conseguiam abrir, porque o ferrolho ficava do lado das crianças. Morreram 183, de 3 a 14 anos. O inquérito levou a uma lei que exigiu saídas de emergência abrindo para fora em locais de espetáculo, e Robert Alexander Briggs, motivado pelo desastre, inventou a tranca com barra horizontal, patenteada em 1892. Nos Estados Unidos, pelo menos 602 pessoas morreram em 1903 no incêndio do Iroquois Theatre, em Chicago, em boa parte por causa de trincos difíceis de abrir. Carl Prinzler, gerente de um setor de ferragens numa loja de Indianápolis, que por acaso escapou de estar entre as vítimas, desenvolveu com o arquiteto Henry H. Dupont uma barra que destrava a porta trancada com uma simples pressão por dentro.

fontes.trecho: On 16 June 1883, a crowd crush caused by the distribution of free prizes resulted in the deaths of 183 children at the Victoria Hall in Sunderland, England. [...] a children's variety show was presented by the travelling entertainer Alexander Fay [...] At the show's end, an announcement was made that children with certain numbered tickets would be presented with a prize upon exit. At the same time, entertainers began distributing gifts from the stage to the children in the stalls. Worried about missing out on the treats, many of the estimated 1,100 children in the gallery surged toward the staircase leading downstairs. At the bottom of the staircase, the door opened inward and had been bolted to leave a gap only wide enough for one child to pass at a time. It is believed this was to ensure the orderly checking of tickets. [...] Those at the front became trapped and were crushed to death by the weight of the crowd behind them. When the adults in the auditorium realised what was happening, they rushed to the door but could not open it as the bolt was on the children's side. [...] killed 183 children between 3 and 14 years of age. [...] The resulting inquiry led to legislation that public entertainment venues be fitted with a minimum number of outward-opening emergency exits, which led to the invention of "push bar" emergency doors.

While originally conceived as a way to prevent crowd crushing in an emergency, crash bars are now used as the primary door opening mechanism in many commercial buildings. [...] Motivated by the Victoria Hall disaster, Robert Alexander Briggs (1868–1963) invented the panic bolt mechanism with horizontal bar which was granted a UK patent on 13 August 1892. [...] in the United States, at least 602 people died in the Iroquois Theatre fire in Chicago in December 1903 because of door latch designs that were difficult for fleeing patrons to open. A survivor of the Iroquois Theater fire, Carl Prinzler, along with architect Henry H. Dupont, independently developed and were awarded a series of nine patents relating to new and improved exit door hardware. All of the patent designs focused on a single lever bar (and related hardware) that would cause a locked door to pop open when simple interior pressure was exerted upon it.

Carl Jacob Prinzler (June 6, 1870 – May 30, 1949) was an American engineer who invented the "panic bar"  device for doors that allowed them to be opened from the inside despite being locked on the outside. He was manager of the Builders Hardware Department at the Vonnegut Hardware Company in 1903, when, along with his architect and engineer neighbor Henry H. DuPont, he developed the first panic bar. [...] found employment as a sales clerk at the Lilly and Stalnaker Hardware Company in downtown Indianapolis. [...] Prinzler had been in Chicago on December 30, 1903, and, by some fortunate twist of fate, escaped becoming a victim of the tragic Iroquois Theatre Fire which claimed 600 lives. [...] All of the patent designs focused on a single lever bar (and related hardware) that would cause a locked door to pop open when simple interior pressure was exerted upon it.

gancho: A dança indiana Bharatanatyam, condenada por missionários e autoridades coloniais, foi revivida nos anos 1930 por Rukmini Devi, e o empurrão veio de uma bailarina russa: Anna Pavlova.
explicacao: A dança, então chamada sadiraattam, era ligada sobretudo aos templos hindus tâmeis até o século XIX. Missionários cristãos e funcionários coloniais apresentavam as dançarinas dos templos, as devadasis, como prova de uma cultura degradada, e em 1892 surgiu um movimento "antidança" que a acusava de acobertar a prostituição. A campanha e as restrições provocaram protestos, e a arte foi levada para fora dos templos. Em 1932, foi rebatizada de Bharatanatyam. Uma das figuras centrais foi Rukmini Devi, nascida em 1904 numa família brâmane tâmil. Em 1928, ela e o marido assistiram a Anna Pavlova em Bombaim e, por acaso, viajaram no mesmo navio que a bailarina rumo à Austrália. Ficaram amigos, Rukmini começou a ter aulas com uma solista da companhia e, a pedido de Pavlova, voltou-se para as danças tradicionais indianas que tinham caído em descrédito. Em 1935 fez sua primeira apresentação pública e, em 1936, fundou em Chennai a Kalakshetra, academia de dança e música. Mas o renascimento também mudou o público da dança, que passou a mirar as moças de classe média e alta.

fontes.trecho: Sadiraattam, which was renamed Bharatanatyam in 1932, is the oldest classical dance tradition in India. [...] Sadiraattam remained exclusive to Tamil Hindu temples through the 19th century. It was banned by the colonial British government in 1910, but the Indian community protested against the ban and expanded its performance outside temples in the 20th century as Bharatanatyam. [...] Christian missionaries and British officials presented "nautch girls" of north India (Kathak) and "devadasis" of south India (Bharatanatyam) as evidence of a "harlots, debased erotic culture, slavery to idols and priests" tradition. The Christian missionaries demanded that this be stopped, launching the "anti-dance movement" in 1892. The anti-dance camp accused the dance form of being a front for prostitution [...] In 1910, the Madras Presidency of the British Empire banned temple dancing, and with it the classical dance tradition in Hindu temples. [...] Figures such as Rukmini Devi Arundale, who is credited with revitalizing Bharatanatyam, also shifted the practice to appeal to middle- and upper-class women.

Rukmini Devi was born in British Raj India in a Tamil Brahmin family on 29 February 1904 in Madurai of Tamil Nadu. [...] In 1928, the famous Russian ballerina Anna Pavlova visited Bombay and the Arundale couple went to her performance, and later happened to travel on the same ship as her, to Australia where she was to perform next; over the course of the journey their friendship grew, and soon Rukmini Devi started learning dance from one of Anna's leading solo dancers, Cleo Nordi. It was later, at the behest of Anna, that Rukmini Devi turned her attention to discovering traditional Indian dance forms which had fallen to disrepute, and dedicated the rest of her life to their revival. [...] In 1935, Rukmini Devi gave her first public performance at the 'Diamond Jubilee Convention of the Theosophical Society. In January 1936, she along with her husband, established Kalakshetra, an academy of dance and music

gancho: As primeiras atrizes profissionais conhecidas na Europa desde a Antiguidade surgiram na commedia dell'arte, nos anos 1560. Na Inglaterra, só chegaram aos palcos profissionais cerca de um século depois, nos anos 1660.
explicacao: Na commedia dell'arte, teatro de improviso com personagens fixos, os papéis femininos eram feitos por mulheres desde os anos 1560. Lucrezia Di Siena, cujo nome aparece num contrato de atores de 10 de outubro de 1564, é apontada como a primeira atriz italiana conhecida pelo nome. A novidade incomodou. Nos anos 1570, críticos ingleses desdenhavam das trupes com atrizes, e prelados italianos tentaram bani-las, mas no fim do século XVI elas já eram comuns nos palcos da Itália. A mais famosa foi Isabella Andreini, contratada aos catorze anos, em 1576, pela companhia dos Gelosi, que se apresentava para a nobreza da Itália e da França, inclusive para o rei Henrique III. Especialista no papel da jovem apaixonada, ajudou a desenvolver a improvisação e passou a dividir com o marido a direção da trupe; a personagem Isabella da commedia ganhou o nome dela. Na Inglaterra, o teatro foi proibido no governo puritano e, com a volta da monarquia, as licenças das companhias, reeditadas em 1662, passaram a permitir formalmente que atrizes se apresentassem.

fontes.trecho: In commedia dell'arte, female roles were played by women, documented as early as the 1560s, making them the first known professional actresses in Europe since antiquity. Lucrezia Di Siena, whose name is on a contract of actors from 10 October 1564, has been referred to as the first Italian actress known by name [...] In the 1570s, English theatre critics generally denigrated the troupes with their female actors [...] By the end of the 1570s, Italian prelates attempted to ban female performers; however, by the end of the 16th century, actresses were standard on the Italian stage.

The role of Isabella of the commedia dell'arte was named after her. [...] In 1576, at age fourteen, Andreini was hired by the troupe of Flaminio Scala, the Compagnia dei Comici Gelosi. [...] The Gelosi were patronised by the aristocracy of northern Italy, usually performing for the gentry of Italy and France. Henry III of France was fond of the troupe, and Andreini performed for him in those very early years. From the beginning, Andreini particularly performed the role of the enamoured woman, the prima donna innamorata [...] She was one of the women who introduced, developed, and excelled at improvisation. [...] Together with her husband, she managed the troupe's activities and negotiated with potential patrons.

Public entertainments, such as theatrical performances, were banned under the Puritan rule in the English Commonwealth. [...] The letters patent were reissued in 1662 with revisions allowing actresses to perform for the first time.
